reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / vasculitis guidance
clinicalPearls: Chronic urticarial vasculitis with persistently low complement and systemic involvement, often more severe than the normocomplementaemic form
Anti-C1q antibodies are characteristic and closely linked to complement consumption
Systemic features include arthritis, angio-oedema, obstructive lung disease, ocular inflammation, and glomerulonephritis
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, often accelerated by smoking, is an important cause of morbidity and mortality
There is substantial overlap with systemic lupus erythematosus, and some patients meet criteria for both
Markedly reduced C1q with low C3 and C4 supports the diagnosis
Management uses immunosuppression and glucocorticoids directed at the systemic burden of disease
reference.pathophysiology: Hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome is driven by autoantibodies against the collagen-like region of C1q. These anti-C1q antibodies form immune complexes that activate the classical complement pathway, consuming C1q, C4, and C3 and generating a small-vessel leucocytoclastic vasculitis. Immune complex deposition and complement activation extend beyond the skin to the joints, kidneys, eyes, and lungs, producing the multisystem phenotype. The overlap with lupus reflects shared immune-complex and complement-mediated mechanisms.
additionalInvestigations: Complement panel showing low C1q, C3, and C4
Skin biopsy with histology and direct immunofluorescence
Antinuclear antibody and anti-double-stranded DNA to assess lupus overlap
Renal function and urinalysis for glomerulonephritis
Pulmonary function tests and chest imaging for obstructive lung disease
redFlags: Progressive obstructive lung disease with respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: The syndrome tends to be chronic and relapsing with a higher systemic burden than normocomplementaemic disease; pulmonary and renal involvement drive long-term morbidity and mortality, and smoking markedly worsens the obstructive lung disease. Immunosuppression can control inflammation but the course is often protracted.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis by not measuring complement in chronic urticaria-like rashes
Failing to assess for renal and pulmonary involvement
Not recognising overlap with systemic lupus erythematosus
Neglecting smoking cessation despite its impact on the obstructive lung disease
references: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference vasculitis nomenclature
